issues.subcategory: Simulated/dummy data used for all analyses
issues.description: The entire results section is based on randomly generated dummy data from Qualtrics (N=1000), not actual participant data. All reported statistics, effect sizes, p-values, and conclusions are meaningless artifacts of random number generation. The manuscript presents these results as if they are interpretable findings, including drawing conclusions about hypotheses (e.g., 'no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning') and making comparisons to the original study. This fundamentally undermines every claim in the paper.
issues.quote: Method and results sections were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.

issues.subcategory: Self-selection into conditions instead of random assignment
issues.description: The procedures state that participants 'selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions,' which means there is no random assignment. This fundamentally compromises the experimental design, introduces self-selection bias, and makes causal inference impossible. The original study used random assignment. This is a critical deviation that undermines the entire replication.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent description of design (within-subject vs. between-subject)
issues.description: The design section states this is a 'single within-subject design,' but the original studies used between-subjects designs, the analysis uses between-subjects ANOVA, and the descriptive statistics show different sample sizes per cell (consistent with between-subjects). A within-subject design would be a major departure from the original and would introduce order effects and demand characteristics. This appears to be a labeling error, but it creates confusion about the actual design.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables

issues.subcategory: Removal of real monetary donation (hypothetical vs. real)
issues.description: The original study gave participants $5 and measured actual donation behavior. This replication uses imaginary/hypothetical donation ($0-$5 scale). This is a significant deviation that changes the dependent variable from a behavioral measure to a self-report measure, which may substantially affect results due to hypothetical bias. This undermines the claim of a 'close to very close replication.'
issues.quote: Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.subcategory: Merging two separate studies into one
issues.description: Studies 1 and 3 of the original article were separate experiments with different designs and manipulations. Merging them into a single experiment with a 2×3 design changes the experimental structure substantially. Study 1 used explicit teaching about the identifiable victim effect, while Study 3 used implicit activation through joint presentation. Combining these creates a hybrid design that may not adequately test either original study's hypotheses.
issues.quote: In this replication, we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment to study both the explicit and implicit intervention of debiasing the identifiable victim effect

issues.subcategory: Abstract draws conclusions from dummy data
issues.description: The abstract states substantive conclusions ('found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning' and 'Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact') based on randomly generated data. These conclusions are presented as actual findings despite the disclaimer that data is simulated.
issues.quote: We generated a dummy set of samples in the Qualtrics survey (N = 1000) and found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent descriptive statistics in results text vs. tables
issues.description: In the results text discussing Table 10, the authors report that participants facing statistical victims donated more (M=2.54, SD=1.76) than those facing identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67). However, Table 7 shows different values: identifiable victim conditions have means of 2.58 and 2.50, and statistical victim conditions have means of 2.46 and 2.01. The values reported in the text do not match any values in the descriptive statistics table.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67)

issues.subcategory: Direction of identifiable victim effect reversed
issues.description: The replication finds that statistical victims received MORE donations than identifiable victims, which is the opposite direction of the identifiable victim effect and the opposite of Hypothesis 1. Yet this is not clearly flagged as a reversal in the results section. The original study found identifiable victims received more (M=2.12 vs M=1.21), while the replication text reports statistical victims received more (M=2.54 vs M=2.24).
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67)

issues.subcategory: Unrealistic age range in dummy data
issues.description: The dummy data shows an age range of 18-120 years with a mean of 67.8 and SD of 30.10. An age of 120 is biologically implausible, and the mean age of ~68 is unrealistic for any typical participant sample. While this is acknowledged as dummy data, it suggests no data cleaning or validation procedures are in place.
issues.quote: Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males

issues.subcategory: Missing power analysis details in main text
issues.description: The manuscript references a power analysis in the supplementary materials but does not report the target sample size, expected effect size, or achieved power in the main text. The reader cannot evaluate whether the study is adequately powered without accessing external materials.
issues.quote: The full report of power analysis can be found in the supplementary under the section of "Power analysis of the original study effect".

issues.subcategory: No compensation mentioned for replication participants
issues.description: The original study compensated participants with $5 (which also served as the donation pool). The replication states compensation is 'Not specified.' The absence of real monetary stakes fundamentally changes the decision context and incentive structure, which is particularly problematic for a study about donation behavior.
issues.quote: Compensation | US$5 | Not specified | Not specified

issues.subcategory: Missing exclusion criteria details
issues.description: The manuscript mentions excluding participants with prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect and those who failed attention checks, but does not specify how many participants were excluded, what the attention check consisted of, or how prior knowledge was assessed.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.subcategory: Incorrect degrees of freedom in original study Table 1
issues.description: Table 1 reports df2=115 for a 2×2 ANOVA with N=121. With 4 cells and N=121, the residual df should be 121-4=117, not 115. This suggests either the original N was different, there were exclusions, or the df is incorrectly reported.
issues.quote:
df1 | df2 | F | p | ηp2
Identifiability |  |  | 1 | 115 | 6.75 | <.05*

issues.subcategory: Extension hypothesis direction contradicted by results
issues.description: Hypothesis 6 predicts that identifiable victims elicit higher perceived impact than statistical victims. However, the significant post-hoc result found is between statistical and joint conditions (not identifiable vs. statistical), and it shows statistical victims had HIGHER perceived impact (M=3.12) than the joint condition (M=2.85). This contradicts the theoretical prediction and the hypothesis, yet the authors do not discuss this discrepancy.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=3.12, SD=1.43) had a higher rating of perceived impact of their donation to help the victims than they faced an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics (M=2.85, SD=1.34)

issues.subcategory: No discussion section
issues.description: The manuscript lacks a discussion section entirely. There is no interpretation of findings, no comparison of replication results to original findings using the stated evaluation criteria (Lebel et al., 2019), no discussion of limitations, and no consideration of what the results mean for the identifiable victim effect literature.

issues.subcategory: Replication classification overclaim
issues.description: The replication is classified as 'close to very close' despite multiple substantial deviations: hypothetical instead of real donations, online instead of lab setting, no monetary compensation, merging two studies into one, adding intervention to the joint condition, different participant population (MTurk vs. university students), and self-selection into conditions. These collectively represent far more than minor deviations.
issues.quote: Replication classification | close to very close replication

issues.subcategory: Applying intervention to joint condition changes Study 3 design
issues.description: The original Study 3 did not include any explicit intervention (teaching about the identifiable victim effect). By applying the intervention to the joint condition, the replication fundamentally changes the design of Study 3, making it impossible to test the original hypothesis about implicit debiasing through joint presentation alone.
issues.quote: The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition to reveal a more comprehensive comparison between the explicit and implicit settings.

issues.subcategory: Table 4 has redundant columns
issues.description: Table 4 comparing original and replication samples has three columns but the last two appear identical (both showing the same Qualtrics-generated data). This appears to be a formatting error.
issues.quote: Sample size | Study 1: 121 Study 3: 159 | 1000 | 1000

issues.subcategory: Omission of ordered probit regression without justification
issues.description: The original study used ordered probit regression as one of its analyses. The replication explicitly states this will not be conducted but provides no justification for omitting it. This selective omission of an analytical approach could affect the comparability of results.
issues.quote: Ordered probit regression | a. effect of identifiability on donation | This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.subcategory: Post-hoc test significant but effect size CI includes zero
issues.description: In Table 10, the identifiable vs. statistical comparison is reported as significant (p=.049) with d=0.076, but the 95% CI for the effect size is [-0.05, 0.20], which includes zero. While p-values and CIs can technically diverge slightly due to different calculations, this borderline result with a CI spanning zero raises concerns about the reliability of the finding.

issues.subcategory: Causal claims from non-randomized design
issues.description: Given that participants self-selected into conditions rather than being randomly assigned, no causal inferences can be drawn from the results. Yet the hypotheses and analytical framework are structured to test causal claims about the effects of identifiability and intervention on donation.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.subcategory: Missing details on attention check and manipulation check
issues.description: The manuscript mentions an attention check but provides no details about what it consisted of, how it was scored, or what the pass/fail rate was. There is also no mention of manipulation checks to verify that the intervention (teaching about the identifiable victim effect) was understood by participants.

issues.subcategory: Missing reliability information for feeling measures
issues.description: The aggregated feelings measure combines multiple items (upsetting, sympathy, touched, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact), but no reliability statistics (e.g., Cronbach's alpha) are reported for this composite measure.

issues.subcategory: Hypothesis 5a prediction contradicted by extension results
issues.description: Hypothesis 5a states that identifiable victims elicit more affective feelings than statistical victims and the joint condition. However, the extension results show that statistical victims actually produced higher perceived impact ratings than the joint condition, and no differences were found for other feelings. The manuscript does not reconcile these findings with the hypothesis.
issues.quote: An identifiable victim elicits more affective feelings than an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics and statistical victims

issues.subcategory: Mischaracterization of availability heuristic
issues.description: The manuscript describes the 'availability heuristic' as the mechanism activated when valuing a personalized individual, but the availability heuristic specifically refers to judging frequency or probability based on ease of recall. What the authors are describing is closer to the affect heuristic or vividness effects. The citation to Tversky & Kahneman (1973) is about the availability heuristic for frequency judgments, not emotional responses to identified individuals.
issues.quote: The "availability heuristic" (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973), which relies on the ease of retrieving relevant instances from memory, is believed to be activated when we value a personalized individual

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent spelling of Slovic throughout manuscript
issues.description: The author Paul Slovic's name is repeatedly misspelled as 'Solvic' in the introduction, which also creates incorrect citations.
issues.quote: Solvic (2007) argued for the drawbacks of the phenomenon

issues.subcategory: Online vs. laboratory setting confound
issues.description: The shift from a controlled laboratory setting to an online MTurk survey introduces numerous potential confounds including reduced attention, multitasking, different environmental contexts, and reduced experimental control. This is particularly relevant for a study involving emotional responses and donation decisions.
issues.quote: Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study surveyed inside a student center of a university in Pennsylvania

issues.subcategory: Unequal cell sizes not addressed
issues.description: The descriptive statistics in Table 7 show unequal cell sizes ranging from 159 to 175 across the six conditions. The manuscript does not explain why cell sizes are unequal (which would be unusual for random assignment) or whether this was addressed in the analyses (e.g., Type III sums of squares).

issues.subcategory: Total N does not match stated sample
issues.description: The stated sample size is N=1000, but summing the cell sizes from Table 7 gives 159+175+166+175+159+166=1000. However, after exclusions for prior knowledge and failed attention checks (mentioned in the methods), the analyzed N should be less than 1000. Either no exclusions were applied or the stated N of 1000 is post-exclusion, which is not clarified.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration... Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.
